questions.q:
A $16 \text{ g}$ sample of a hydrocarbon exactly requires $64 \text{ g}$ of oxygen gas for complete combustion. The products formed are carbon dioxide and water. When the carbon dioxide gas formed is completely absorbed in an aqueous $\text{KOH}$ solution, the mass of the solution increases by $44 \text{ g}$.
Consider the following statements regarding this process:
(A) The total mass of the products formed is $80 \text{ g}$.
(B) The mass of water formed during the combustion is $36 \text{ g}$.
(C) The mass of carbon present in the hydrocarbon sample is $16 \text{ g}$.
(D) The empirical formula of the hydrocarbon is $\text{CH}_4$.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.question:
A $16 \text{ g}$ sample of a hydrocarbon exactly requires $64 \text{ g}$ of oxygen gas for complete combustion. The products formed are carbon dioxide and water. When the carbon dioxide gas formed is completely absorbed in an aqueous $\text{KOH}$ solution, the mass of the solution increases by $44 \text{ g}$.
Consider the following statements regarding this process:
(A) The total mass of the products formed is $80 \text{ g}$.
(B) The mass of water formed during the combustion is $36 \text{ g}$.
(C) The mass of carbon present in the hydrocarbon sample is $16 \text{ g}$.
(D) The empirical formula of the hydrocarbon is $\text{CH}_4$.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
According to the law of conservation of mass, the total mass of the products is equal to the total mass of the reactants.

Total mass of products = Mass of hydrocarbon + Mass of oxygen = $16 \text{ g} + 64 \text{ g} = 80 \text{ g}$.

Thus, statement (A) is correct.

The carbon dioxide formed is absorbed by the aqueous $\text{KOH}$ solution. The increase in the mass of the solution corresponds to the mass of $\text{CO}_2$ absorbed.

Mass of $\text{CO}_2$ formed = $44 \text{ g}$.

Mass of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ formed = Total mass of products - Mass of $\text{CO}_2$ = $80 \text{ g} - 44 \text{ g} = 36 \text{ g}$.

Thus, statement (B) is correct.

The mass of carbon in the hydrocarbon is equal to the mass of carbon in the $\text{CO}_2$ formed.

Mass of carbon = $\dfrac{12}{44} \times 44 \text{ g} = 12 \text{ g}$.

Thus, statement (C) is incorrect.

The mass of hydrogen in the hydrocarbon is equal to the mass of hydrogen in the $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ formed.

Mass of hydrogen = $\dfrac{2}{18} \times 36 \text{ g} = 4 \text{ g}$.

Moles of carbon = $\dfrac{12}{12} = 1 \text{ mol}$.

Moles of hydrogen = $\dfrac{4}{1} = 4 \text{ mol}$.

The molar ratio of $\text{C} : \text{H}$ is $1 : 4$. The empirical formula of the hydrocarbon is $\text{CH}_4$.

Thus, statement (D) is correct.

The correct statements are (A), (B), and (D).

Answer: (A), (B) and (D) only

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A $15.5\text{ g}$ sample of an impure carbonate ore is treated with $50.0\text{ mL}$ of an aqueous acid solution (density $1.10\text{ g mL}^{-1}$). After the reaction ceases, the combined mass of the remaining solution and the undissolved material is $66.1\text{ g}$. Carbon dioxide gas is evolved during the process. If the density of the evolved gas is $2.20\text{ g L}^{-1}$ under the experimental conditions, what is the volume of the gas released?
questions.question: A $15.5\text{ g}$ sample of an impure carbonate ore is treated with $50.0\text{ mL}$ of an aqueous acid solution (density $1.10\text{ g mL}^{-1}$). After the reaction ceases, the combined mass of the remaining solution and the undissolved material is $66.1\text{ g}$. Carbon dioxide gas is evolved during the process. If the density of the evolved gas is $2.20\text{ g L}^{-1}$ under the experimental conditions, what is the volume of the gas released?
questions.solution:
Mass of the aqueous acid solution is calculated by multiplying its volume and density.

Mass of acid solution $= 50.0 \text{ mL} \times 1.10 \text{ g mL}^{-1} = 55.0 \text{ g}$

Total initial mass of the reactants is the sum of the mass of the impure carbonate ore and the mass of the acid solution.

Total initial mass $= 15.5 \text{ g} + 55.0 \text{ g} = 70.5 \text{ g}$

According to the law of conservation of mass, the mass of the evolved carbon dioxide gas is the difference between the total initial mass and the final mass of the remaining contents.

Mass of evolved gas $= 70.5 \text{ g} - 66.1 \text{ g} = 4.4 \text{ g}$

The volume of the evolved gas is obtained by dividing its mass by its density.

Volume of gas $= \dfrac{4.4 \text{ g}}{2.20 \text{ g L}^{-1}} = 2.0 \text{ L}$

Answer: $2.0\text{ L}$

Volume of gas $= \dfrac{4.4 \text{ g}}{2.20 \text{ g L}^{-1}} = 2.0 \text{ L}$

Answer: $2.0\text{ L}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: When a mixture of aluminium powder and chromium(III) oxide is ignited, it produces chromium metal and aluminium oxide. In an experiment, $10.8\text{ g}$ of aluminium was mixed with $40.0\text{ g}$ of chromium(III) oxide. At the end of the reaction, the mixture contained $20.8\text{ g}$ of chromium, $20.4\text{ g}$ of aluminium oxide, and an undetermined amount of unreacted chromium(III) oxide. If no aluminium was left, what is the mass of the unreacted chromium(III) oxide? (Assume no mass is lost during the reaction)
questions.question: When a mixture of aluminium powder and chromium(III) oxide is ignited, it produces chromium metal and aluminium oxide. In an experiment, $10.8\text{ g}$ of aluminium was mixed with $40.0\text{ g}$ of chromium(III) oxide. At the end of the reaction, the mixture contained $20.8\text{ g}$ of chromium, $20.4\text{ g}$ of aluminium oxide, and an undetermined amount of unreacted chromium(III) oxide. If no aluminium was left, what is the mass of the unreacted chromium(III) oxide? (Assume no mass is lost during the reaction)
questions.solution:
According to the law of conservation of mass, the total mass before the reaction is equal to the total mass after the reaction.

Total initial mass $= \text{Mass of aluminium} + \text{Mass of chromium(III) oxide}$

Total initial mass $= 10.8\text{ g} + 40.0\text{ g} = 50.8\text{ g}$

Total final mass $= \text{Mass of chromium} + \text{Mass of aluminium oxide} + \text{Mass of unreacted chromium(III) oxide}$

Total final mass $= 20.8\text{ g} + 20.4\text{ g} + x = 41.2\text{ g} + x$

Equating the initial and final masses:

$50.8\text{ g} = 41.2\text{ g} + x$

$x = 50.8\text{ g} - 41.2\text{ g} = 9.6\text{ g}$

Answer: $9.6\text{ g}$

Answer: $9.6\text{ g}$

Consider the following statements for an aqueous solution of ethanol having a total volume of $45.0\text{ mL}$ and a total mass of $40.0\text{ g}$. Assume that there is no change in volume when the pure components are mixed. (Given: Density of pure ethanol $= 0.80\text{ g mL}^{-1}$, Density of water $= 1.00\text{ g mL}^{-1}$, Molar mass of ethanol $= 46\text{ g mol}^{-1}$, Molar mass of water $= 18\text{ g mol}^{-1}$)

(A) The volume of ethanol in the solution is $25.0\text{ mL}$.
(B) The mass of water in the solution is $25.0\text{ g}$.
(C) The mass percentage of ethanol in the solution is $50\%$.
(D) The mole fraction of ethanol in the solution is greater than $0.5$.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.question:
Consider the following statements for an aqueous solution of ethanol having a total volume of $45.0\text{ mL}$ and a total mass of $40.0\text{ g}$. Assume that there is no change in volume when the pure components are mixed. (Given: Density of pure ethanol $= 0.80\text{ g mL}^{-1}$, Density of water $= 1.00\text{ g mL}^{-1}$, Molar mass of ethanol $= 46\text{ g mol}^{-1}$, Molar mass of water $= 18\text{ g mol}^{-1}$)

(A) The volume of ethanol in the solution is $25.0\text{ mL}$.
(B) The mass of water in the solution is $25.0\text{ g}$.
(C) The mass percentage of ethanol in the solution is $50\%$.
(D) The mole fraction of ethanol in the solution is greater than $0.5$.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
Let the volume of ethanol be $V_{E}$ and the volume of water be $V_{W}$.

Given that the total volume is $45.0\text{ mL}$:
$V_{E} + V_{W} = 45.0$

The total mass of the solution is $40.0\text{ g}$:
$0.80 V_{E} + 1.00 V_{W} = 40.0$

Subtracting the second equation from the first equation:
$0.20 V_{E} = 5.0 \Rightarrow V_{E} = 25.0\text{ mL}$

Thus, the volume of ethanol is $25.0\text{ mL}$. Statement (A) is correct.

The volume of water is $V_{W} = 45.0 - 25.0 = 20.0\text{ mL}$.
The mass of water is $20.0 \times 1.00 = 20.0\text{ g}$. Statement (B) is incorrect.

The mass of ethanol is $25.0 \times 0.80 = 20.0\text{ g}$.
The mass percentage of ethanol is $\dfrac{20.0}{40.0} \times 100 = 50\%$. Statement (C) is correct.

The number of moles of ethanol is $n_{E} = \dfrac{20.0}{46} \approx 0.43\text{ mol}$.
The number of moles of water is $n_{W} = \dfrac{20.0}{18} \approx 1.11\text{ mol}$.
Since $n_{E} < n_{W}$, the mole fraction of ethanol is less than $0.5$. Statement (D) is incorrect.

Therefore, only statements (A) and (C) are correct.

Answer: (A) and (C) only

questions.q: An aqueous solution containing $5\%$ (by mass) of a non-volatile solute is concentrated by evaporation. After a certain amount of water is evaporated, the concentration of the solute in the remaining solution becomes $25\%$ (by mass). If $400\text{ g}$ of the initial solution is taken, the mass of water evaporated is:
questions.question: An aqueous solution containing $5\%$ (by mass) of a non-volatile solute is concentrated by evaporation. After a certain amount of water is evaporated, the concentration of the solute in the remaining solution becomes $25\%$ (by mass). If $400\text{ g}$ of the initial solution is taken, the mass of water evaporated is:
questions.solution:
Initial mass of the solution = $400\text{ g}$

Initial mass of the non-volatile solute = $5\%$ of $400\text{ g} = \dfrac{5}{100} \times 400 = 20\text{ g}$

Since the solute is non-volatile, its mass remains constant during evaporation.

Let the final mass of the solution be $M_f$.

Given that the final concentration of the solute is $25\%$ by mass:

$\dfrac{25}{100} \times M_f = 20$

$M_f = \dfrac{20 \times 100}{25} = 80\text{ g}$

The mass of water evaporated is the difference between the initial and final mass of the solution.

Mass of water evaporated = $400\text{ g} - 80\text{ g} = 320\text{ g}$

Answer: $320\text{ g}$

questions.q: At $373\text{ K}$ and $1\text{ atm}$ pressure, the density of liquid water is $1.0\text{ g mL}^{-1}$ and that of water vapour is $6.0 \times 10^{-4}\text{ g mL}^{-1}$. Assuming that water molecules are closely packed in the liquid state, the actual volume occupied by the water molecules in $5\text{ L}$ of steam at the same temperature and pressure is:
questions.question: At $373\text{ K}$ and $1\text{ atm}$ pressure, the density of liquid water is $1.0\text{ g mL}^{-1}$ and that of water vapour is $6.0 \times 10^{-4}\text{ g mL}^{-1}$. Assuming that water molecules are closely packed in the liquid state, the actual volume occupied by the water molecules in $5\text{ L}$ of steam at the same temperature and pressure is:
questions.solution:
The mass of $5\text{ L}$ of steam is calculated using its density.

Mass of steam = Volume $\times$ Density of water vapour

Mass of steam = $5000\text{ mL} \times 6.0 \times 10^{-4}\text{ g mL}^{-1} = 3.0\text{ g}$

Since water molecules are closely packed in the liquid state, the actual volume occupied by the molecules is equal to the volume of this mass in the liquid state.

Volume of liquid water = $\dfrac{\text{Mass}}{\text{Density of liquid water}}$

Volume = $\dfrac{3.0\text{ g}}{1.0\text{ g mL}^{-1}} = 3.0\text{ mL}$

Answer: $3.0\text{ mL}$
questions.explanation:
The mass of $5\text{ L}$ of steam is calculated using its density.

Mass of steam = Volume $\times$ Density of water vapour

Mass of steam = $5000\text{ mL} \times 6.0 \times 10^{-4}\text{ g mL}^{-1} = 3.0\text{ g}$

Volume of liquid water = $\dfrac{\text{Mass}}{\text{Density of liquid water}}$

Volume = $\dfrac{3.0\text{ g}}{1.0\text{ g mL}^{-1}} = 3.0\text{ mL}$

Answer: $3.0\text{ mL}$

Consider the following statements regarding the law of multiple proportions:
(A) It is applicable to the oxides of carbon.
(B) It is applicable to the oxides of aluminium.
(C) It is applicable to the oxides of nitrogen.
(D) It is applicable to the oxides of zinc.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding the law of multiple proportions:
(A) It is applicable to the oxides of carbon.
(B) It is applicable to the oxides of aluminium.
(C) It is applicable to the oxides of nitrogen.
(D) It is applicable to the oxides of zinc.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
The law of multiple proportions is applicable when two elements combine to form more than one compound.

Carbon forms multiple oxides such as $CO$ and $CO_2$. Thus, the law of multiple proportions is applicable to the oxides of carbon.

Nitrogen forms multiple oxides such as $N_2O$, $NO$, $N_2O_3$, $NO_2$, and $N_2O_5$. Thus, the law of multiple proportions is applicable to the oxides of nitrogen.

Aluminium and zinc form only one stable oxide each, which are $Al_2O_3$ and $ZnO$ respectively. Thus, the law of multiple proportions is not applicable to them.

Therefore, the correct statements are (A) and (C) only.

Answer: (A) and (C) only

questions.solution:
In compound C, $2\text{ g}$ of P combines with $9\text{ g}$ of Q.

Mass of Q combining with $1\text{ g}$ of P in compound C $= \dfrac{9}{2}\text{ g}$

$x = 30$

Answer: $30$

questions.q:
The mass of $4.0 \times 10^6$ atoms of an element is $1.8 \times 10^{-16} \text{ g}$. The molar atomic mass of the element is:
(Given: $N_A = 6.0 \times 10^{23} \text{ mol}^{-1}$)
questions.question:
The mass of $4.0 \times 10^6$ atoms of an element is $1.8 \times 10^{-16} \text{ g}$. The molar atomic mass of the element is:
(Given: $N_A = 6.0 \times 10^{23} \text{ mol}^{-1}$)
questions.solution:
Mass of $4.0 \times 10^6$ atoms $= 1.8 \times 10^{-16} \text{ g}$

Mass of $1$ atom $= \dfrac{1.8 \times 10^{-16}}{4.0 \times 10^6} \text{ g}$

Molar atomic mass is the mass of $1$ mole of atoms, which contains $N_A$ atoms.

Molar mass $= \dfrac{1.8 \times 10^{-16}}{4.0 \times 10^6} \times 6.0 \times 10^{23} \text{ g mol}^{-1}$

$= \dfrac{1.8 \times 6.0}{4.0} \times 10^{-16 - 6 + 23} \text{ g mol}^{-1}$

$= 2.7 \times 10^1 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$

$= 27 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$

Answer: $27 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$

The plot given below shows the variation of the number of atoms of an element as a function of its mass (in g).

Based on the graph, the molar mass of the element is:
(Given: Avogadro's number $N_A = 6.0 \times 10^{23} \text{ mol}^{-1}$)
questions.question:
The plot given below shows the variation of the number of atoms of an element as a function of its mass (in g).

Based on the graph, the molar mass of the element is:
(Given: Avogadro's number $N_A = 6.0 \times 10^{23} \text{ mol}^{-1}$)
questions.solution:
The number of atoms ($N$) is given by:

$N = \dfrac{W}{M} \times N_A$

where $W$ is the mass, $M$ is the molar mass, and $N_A$ is Avogadro's number.

From the graph of $N$ versus $W$, the slope is:

$\text{Slope} = \tan \theta = \dfrac{N_A}{M}$

Given $\theta = \tan^{-1}(1.5 \times 10^{22})$, we have:

$\text{Slope} = 1.5 \times 10^{22}$

Therefore,

$\dfrac{N_A}{M} = 1.5 \times 10^{22}$

Substituting $N_A = 6.0 \times 10^{23} \text{ mol}^{-1}$:

$\dfrac{6.0 \times 10^{23}}{M} = 1.5 \times 10^{22}$

$M = \dfrac{6.0 \times 10^{23}}{1.5 \times 10^{22}} = 40 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$

Answer: $40 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$

Consider the following statements:
(A) If a line drawn with a graphite pencil weighs $2.4 \times 10^{-10} \text{ g}$, the number of carbon atoms present in it is $1.2 \times 10^{13}$. (Take $N_A = 6.0 \times 10^{23} \text{ mol}^{-1}$)
(B) $1 \text{ mg}$ of diamond contains fewer carbon atoms than $1 \text{ mg}$ of graphite.
(C) The mass of one atom of $^{12}\text{C}$ isotope is exactly $12 \text{ u}$.
(D) $12 \text{ g}$ of $^{14}\text{C}$ isotope contains exactly one mole of carbon atoms.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
For statement (A), the number of moles of carbon is given by $\dfrac{2.4 \times 10^{-10}}{12} = 2 \times 10^{-11} \text{ mol}$.

The number of carbon atoms is $2 \times 10^{-11} \times 6.0 \times 10^{23} = 1.2 \times 10^{13}$. Thus, statement (A) is correct.

For statement (B), both diamond and graphite are allotropes of carbon. Therefore, $1 \text{ mg}$ of diamond and $1 \text{ mg}$ of graphite both contain the same mass of carbon, which means they contain the same number of carbon atoms. Thus, statement (B) is incorrect.

For statement (C), by definition, $1 \text{ u}$ is exactly $\dfrac{1}{12}$th the mass of one atom of $^{12}\text{C}$. Therefore, the mass of one atom of $^{12}\text{C}$ is exactly $12 \text{ u}$. Thus, statement (C) is correct.

For statement (D), the molar mass of the $^{14}\text{C}$ isotope is $14 \text{ g/mol}$. Therefore, $12 \text{ g}$ of $^{14}\text{C}$ contains $\dfrac{12}{14}$ moles of carbon atoms, not exactly one mole. Thus, statement (D) is incorrect.

The correct statements are (A) and (C) only.

Answer: (A) and (C) only

The correct statements are (A) and (C) only.

questions.q: The atomic masses of two elements X and Y are $16$ and $32$ respectively. If $m\text{ g}$ of X contains $N$ atoms, then the number of atoms present in $4m\text{ g}$ of Y is:
questions.question: The atomic masses of two elements X and Y are $16$ and $32$ respectively. If $m\text{ g}$ of X contains $N$ atoms, then the number of atoms present in $4m\text{ g}$ of Y is:
questions.solution:
Number of moles of X in $m\text{ g} = \dfrac{m}{16}$

Number of atoms of X $= \dfrac{m}{16} \times N_A = N$

Number of moles of Y in $4m\text{ g} = \dfrac{4m}{32} = \dfrac{m}{8}$

Number of atoms of Y $= \dfrac{m}{8} \times N_A$

Since $\dfrac{m}{16} \times N_A = N$, we get $\dfrac{m}{8} \times N_A = 2 \times \left(\dfrac{m}{16} \times N_A\right) = 2N$

Answer: $2N$

Answer: $2N$

An unknown element $\text{X}$ forms a nitride with the molecular formula $\text{X}_3\text{N}_2$. If the compound contains $72\%$ of $\text{X}$ by mass, the atomic mass of $\text{X}$ is ____ $\text{g mol}^{-1}$.
(Given: Atomic mass of $\text{N} = 14 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$)
questions.question:
An unknown element $\text{X}$ forms a nitride with the molecular formula $\text{X}_3\text{N}_2$. If the compound contains $72\%$ of $\text{X}$ by mass, the atomic mass of $\text{X}$ is ____ $\text{g mol}^{-1}$.
(Given: Atomic mass of $\text{N} = 14 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$)
questions.solution:
Let the atomic mass of $\text{X}$ be $M$.

The molar mass of the compound $\text{X}_3\text{N}_2$ is $3M + 2(14) = 3M + 28$.

The mass percentage of $\text{X}$ in the compound is given as $72\%$.

$\dfrac{3M}{3M + 28} = \dfrac{72}{100}$

$\dfrac{3M}{3M + 28} = 0.72$

$3M = 2.16M + 20.16$

$0.84M = 20.16$

$M = \dfrac{20.16}{0.84} = 24$

The atomic mass of $\text{X}$ is $24 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$.

Answer: $24$

questions.q: A $5.0 \text{ g}$ sample of a metallic carbonate $\text{XCO}_3$ is completely converted into $5.55 \text{ g}$ of the corresponding chloride $\text{XCl}_2$ upon treatment with excess hydrochloric acid. Given the atomic masses of $\text{C}$, $\text{O}$, and $\text{Cl}$ are $12$, $16$, and $35.5$ respectively, the atomic mass of the element $\text{X}$ is ____.
questions.question: A $5.0 \text{ g}$ sample of a metallic carbonate $\text{XCO}_3$ is completely converted into $5.55 \text{ g}$ of the corresponding chloride $\text{XCl}_2$ upon treatment with excess hydrochloric acid. Given the atomic masses of $\text{C}$, $\text{O}$, and $\text{Cl}$ are $12$, $16$, and $35.5$ respectively, the atomic mass of the element $\text{X}$ is ____.
questions.solution:
Let the atomic mass of the element $\text{X}$ be $M$.

The molar mass of the metallic carbonate $\text{XCO}_3$ is $M + 12 + 3 \times 16 = M + 60$.

The molar mass of the metallic chloride $\text{XCl}_2$ is $M + 2 \times 35.5 = M + 71$.

The chemical reaction is:

$\text{XCO}_3 + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{XCl}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2$

By the principle of conservation of moles of $\text{X}$, the number of moles of $\text{XCO}_3$ is equal to the number of moles of $\text{XCl}_2$.

$\dfrac{5.0}{M + 60} = \dfrac{5.55}{M + 71}$

Cross-multiplying the equation:

$5.0(M + 71) = 5.55(M + 60)$

$5.0M + 355 = 5.55M + 333$

$0.55M = 22$

$M = \dfrac{22}{0.55} = 40$

The atomic mass of the element $\text{X}$ is $40$.

Answer: $40$

$M = \dfrac{22}{0.55} = 40$

The atomic mass of the element $\text{X}$ is $40$.

Answer: $40$

Consider the following statements:
(A) The percentage abundance of $E^{25}$ is $11\%$.
(B) The percentage abundance of $E^{26}$ is $10\%$.
(C) The number of neutrons in the isotope $E^{25}$ is $12$.
(D) The mole fraction of $E^{24}$ in the naturally occurring element is $0.79$.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.question:
An element $E$ (atomic number $12$) occurs in nature as a mixture of three isotopes: $E^{24}$, $E^{25}$ and $E^{26}$. The percentage abundance of $E^{24}$ is $79\%$ and the average atomic mass of the element $E$ is $24.31 \text{ u}$.
Consider the following statements:
(A) The percentage abundance of $E^{25}$ is $11\%$.
(B) The percentage abundance of $E^{26}$ is $10\%$.
(C) The number of neutrons in the isotope $E^{25}$ is $12$.
(D) The mole fraction of $E^{24}$ in the naturally occurring element is $0.79$.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
Let the percentage abundance of $E^{25}$ be $x\%$.

The percentage abundance of $E^{26}$ will be $(100 - 79 - x)\% = (21 - x)\%$.

The average atomic mass is given by:

$M_{avg} = \dfrac{24 \times 79 + 25 \times x + 26 \times (21 - x)}{100}$

$24.31 = \dfrac{1896 + 25x + 546 - 26x}{100}$

$2431 = 2442 - x$

$x = 11$

The percentage abundance of $E^{25}$ is $11\%$.

The percentage abundance of $E^{26}$ is $21 - 11 = 10\%$.

Thus, statements (A) and (B) are correct.

The atomic number of $E$ is $12$. The number of neutrons in $E^{25}$ is $25 - 12 = 13$.

Thus, statement (C) is incorrect.

The percentage abundance of $E^{24}$ is $79\%$, so its mole fraction is $\dfrac{79}{100} = 0.79$.

Thus, statement (D) is correct.

The correct statements are (A), (B), and (D).

Answer: (A), (B) and (D) only

Consider the following statements:
(A) The sample contains exactly $3.0$ moles of atoms.
(B) The total number of atoms in the sample is $1.8066 \times 10^{23}$.
(C) The total number of neutrons present in the sample is $6.022 \times 10^{20}$.
(D) The mass of deuterium present in the sample is $2.0$ mg.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.question:
Consider a $3.001$ g sample of hydrogen gas containing only $^1\text{H}$ and $^2\text{D}$ atoms in an atomic ratio of $2999 : 1$. (Given: atomic mass of $^1\text{H} = 1.0$ u, $^2\text{D} = 2.0$ u, $N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23} \text{ mol}^{-1}$)

Consider the following statements:
(A) The sample contains exactly $3.0$ moles of atoms.
(B) The total number of atoms in the sample is $1.8066 \times 10^{23}$.
(C) The total number of neutrons present in the sample is $6.022 \times 10^{20}$.
(D) The mass of deuterium present in the sample is $2.0$ mg.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
Let the number of moles of $^1\text{H}$ and $^2\text{D}$ atoms be $2999x$ and $x$ respectively.

Total mass of the sample = $(2999x \times 1.0) + (x \times 2.0) = 3001x$ g.

Given mass = $3.001$ g, so $3001x = 3.001 \Rightarrow x = 0.001$ mol.

Total moles of atoms = $2999x + x = 3000x = 3000 \times 0.001 = 3.0$ mol. Statement (A) is correct.

Total number of atoms = $3.0 \times N_A = 3.0 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 1.8066 \times 10^{24}$. Statement (B) is incorrect.

Number of neutrons in $^1\text{H}$ is $0$ and in $^2\text{D}$ is $1$. Total moles of neutrons = moles of $^2\text{D}$ = $x = 0.001$ mol.

Total number of neutrons = $0.001 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 6.022 \times 10^{20}$. Statement (C) is correct.

Mass of deuterium = $x \times 2.0 = 0.001 \times 2.0 = 0.002$ g = $2.0$ mg. Statement (D) is correct.

Thus, statements (A), (C), and (D) are correct.

Answer: (A), (C) and (D) only

If the isotopic distribution of $^{12}\text{C}$ and $^{14}\text{C}$ in a sample is $95.0\%$ and $5.0\%$, respectively, then the number of $^{14}\text{C}$ atoms in $24.2\text{ g}$ of this carbon sample is:
(Given: $N_A = 6.02 \times 10^{23} \text{ mol}^{-1}$)
questions.question:
If the isotopic distribution of $^{12}\text{C}$ and $^{14}\text{C}$ in a sample is $95.0\%$ and $5.0\%$, respectively, then the number of $^{14}\text{C}$ atoms in $24.2\text{ g}$ of this carbon sample is:
(Given: $N_A = 6.02 \times 10^{23} \text{ mol}^{-1}$)
questions.solution:
Average atomic mass of the carbon sample is calculated as:

$M_{avg} = \dfrac{95 \times 12 + 5 \times 14}{100} = \dfrac{1140 + 70}{100} = 12.1 \text{ g/mol}$

Total moles of carbon in $24.2 \text{ g}$ of the sample:

$n = \dfrac{24.2}{12.1} = 2 \text{ mol}$

Since the isotopic abundance of $^{14}\text{C}$ is $5.0\%$, the moles of $^{14}\text{C}$ in the sample is:

$n_{14} = 2 \times \dfrac{5}{100} = 0.1 \text{ mol}$

Number of $^{14}\text{C}$ atoms is:

$N = 0.1 \times N_A = 0.1 \times 6.02 \times 10^{23} = 6.02 \times 10^{22}$

Answer: $6.02 \times 10^{22}$

$M_{avg} = \dfrac{95 \times 12 + 5 \times 14}{100} = \dfrac{1140 + 70}{100} = 12.1 \text{ g/mol}$

$n = \dfrac{24.2}{12.1} = 2 \text{ mol}$

$n_{14} = 2 \times \dfrac{5}{100} = 0.1 \text{ mol}$

Number of $^{14}\text{C}$ atoms is:

$N = 0.1 \times N_A = 0.1 \times 6.02 \times 10^{23} = 6.02 \times 10^{22}$

Answer: $6.02 \times 10^{22}$

questions.q: A sample of copper contains only two isotopes, $^{63}\text{Cu}$ (atomic mass $= 62.9\text{ u}$) and $^{65}\text{Cu}$ (atomic mass $= 64.9\text{ u}$). If the fractional abundance of $^{63}\text{Cu}$ in the sample is $0.70$, the average atomic mass of copper is:
questions.question: A sample of copper contains only two isotopes, $^{63}\text{Cu}$ (atomic mass $= 62.9\text{ u}$) and $^{65}\text{Cu}$ (atomic mass $= 64.9\text{ u}$). If the fractional abundance of $^{63}\text{Cu}$ in the sample is $0.70$, the average atomic mass of copper is:
questions.solution:
The fractional abundance of $^{63}\text{Cu}$ is $0.70$.

The fractional abundance of $^{65}\text{Cu}$ is $1 - 0.70 = 0.30$.

The average atomic mass is calculated as the sum of the products of the fractional abundances and their respective atomic masses.

Average atomic mass $= (0.70 \times 62.9) + (0.30 \times 64.9)$

Average atomic mass $= 44.03 + 19.47 = 63.5\text{ u}$

Answer: $63.5\text{ u}$

questions.q:
How many molecules of water ($\text{H}_2\text{O}$) will weigh exactly as much as $10$ molecules of glucose ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6$)?
(Given atomic masses in $\text{u}$: $\text{H} = 1$, $\text{C} = 12$, $\text{O} = 16$)
questions.question:
How many molecules of water ($\text{H}_2\text{O}$) will weigh exactly as much as $10$ molecules of glucose ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6$)?
(Given atomic masses in $\text{u}$: $\text{H} = 1$, $\text{C} = 12$, $\text{O} = 16$)
questions.solution:
Molecular mass of glucose ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6$) = $6 \times 12 + 12 \times 1 + 6 \times 16 = 180 \text{ u}$

Mass of $10$ molecules of glucose = $10 \times 180 = 1800 \text{ u}$

Molecular mass of water ($\text{H}_2\text{O}$) = $2 \times 1 + 16 = 18 \text{ u}$

Let $n$ be the number of water molecules.

Mass of $n$ molecules of water = $n \times 18 \text{ u}$

Equating the masses:

$n \times 18 = 1800$

$n = \dfrac{1800}{18} = 100$

Answer: $100$

(Given: Molar mass of $\text{N} = 14\text{ g mol}^{-1}$, $\text{O} = 16\text{ g mol}^{-1}$)
questions.question:
A gaseous mixture of $\text{N}_2$ and $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ is prepared such that it contains an equal number of molecules of each gas. If the mass of $\text{N}_2$ in the mixture is $14\text{ g}$, the mass of $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ present is:
(Given: Molar mass of $\text{N} = 14\text{ g mol}^{-1}$, $\text{O} = 16\text{ g mol}^{-1}$)
questions.solution:
Molar mass of $\text{N}_2 = 2 \times 14 = 28\text{ g mol}^{-1}$

Molar mass of $\text{N}_2\text{O} = 2 \times 14 + 16 = 44\text{ g mol}^{-1}$

Number of moles of $\text{N}_2 = \dfrac{14}{28} = 0.5\text{ mol}$

Since the mixture contains an equal number of molecules of each gas, the number of moles of $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ is equal to the number of moles of $\text{N}_2$.

Number of moles of $\text{N}_2\text{O} = 0.5\text{ mol}$

Mass of $\text{N}_2\text{O} = 0.5 \times 44 = 22\text{ g}$

Answer: $22\text{ g}$

A mixture containing $1.5 imes 10^{22}$ molecules of substance A and $3.0 imes 10^{22}$ molecules of substance B has a total mass of $4.20 \text{ g}$. If the molar mass of substance A is $48 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$, the molar mass of substance B is:
(Given : $N_A = 6.0 \times 10^{23} \text{ mol}^{-1}$)
questions.question:
A mixture containing $1.5 imes 10^{22}$ molecules of substance A and $3.0 imes 10^{22}$ molecules of substance B has a total mass of $4.20 \text{ g}$. If the molar mass of substance A is $48 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$, the molar mass of substance B is:
(Given : $N_A = 6.0 \times 10^{23} \text{ mol}^{-1}$)
questions.solution:
Number of moles of substance A, $n_A = \dfrac{1.5 \times 10^{22}}{6.0 \times 10^{23}} = 0.025 \text{ mol}$

Mass of substance A, $m_A = n_A \times M_A = 0.025 \times 48 = 1.2 \text{ g}$

Mass of substance B, $m_B = 4.20 - 1.2 = 3.0 \text{ g}$

Number of moles of substance B, $n_B = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{22}}{6.0 \times 10^{23}} = 0.05 \text{ mol}$

Molar mass of substance B, $M_B = \dfrac{m_B}{n_B} = \dfrac{3.0}{0.05} = 60 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$

Answer: $60 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$

Number of moles of substance A, $n_A = \dfrac{1.5 \times 10^{22}}{6.0 \times 10^{23}} = 0.025 \text{ mol}$

Mass of substance B, $m_B = 4.20 - 1.2 = 3.0 \text{ g}$

Number of moles of substance B, $n_B = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{22}}{6.0 \times 10^{23}} = 0.05 \text{ mol}$

Molar mass of substance B, $M_B = \dfrac{m_B}{n_B} = \dfrac{3.0}{0.05} = 60 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$

Answer: $60 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$

Molar mass of the virus is $M = m \times N_A$

$M = 12 \times 10^{-17} \times 6 \times 10^{23} = 72 \times 10^6 = 7.20 \times 10^7 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$

Answer: $7.20 \times 10^7\text{ g mol}^{-1}$

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
(A) If the density of mercury vapour relative to air (average molar mass $29 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$) is $6.9$, the atomicity of mercury in its vapour state is $1$. (Given atomic mass of $\text{Hg} = 200 \text{ u}$)
(B) The vapour density of $\text{SO}_2$ gas with respect to $\text{O}_2$ gas is $2$.
(C) The vapour density of a given gas with respect to another gas depends on the temperature and pressure at which it is measured.
(D) The molar mass of a gas is equal to half of its vapour density with respect to hydrogen gas.
The number of correct statements is ____.
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) If the density of mercury vapour relative to air (average molar mass $29 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$) is $6.9$, the atomicity of mercury in its vapour state is $1$. (Given atomic mass of $\text{Hg} = 200 \text{ u}$)
(B) The vapour density of $\text{SO}_2$ gas with respect to $\text{O}_2$ gas is $2$.
(C) The vapour density of a given gas with respect to another gas depends on the temperature and pressure at which it is measured.
(D) The molar mass of a gas is equal to half of its vapour density with respect to hydrogen gas.
The number of correct statements is ____.
questions.solution:
Statement (A):
The relative density of a gas with respect to air is given by the ratio of their molar masses.
$M_{\text{Hg vapour}} = \text{Relative density} \times M_{\text{air}} = 6.9 \times 29 = 200.1 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$
Atomicity of mercury $= \dfrac{\text{Molar mass}}{\text{Atomic mass}} = \dfrac{200.1}{200} \approx 1$
Thus, the atomicity of mercury in its vapour state is $1$. Statement (A) is correct.

Statement (B):
The vapour density of $\text{SO}_2$ with respect to $\text{O}_2$ is the ratio of their molar masses.
$\text{Vapour density} = \dfrac{M_{\text{SO}_2}}{M_{\text{O}_2}} = \dfrac{64}{32} = 2$
Statement (B) is correct.

Statement (C):
The vapour density of a gas with respect to another gas is equal to the ratio of their molar masses ($\dfrac{M_1}{M_2}$). Since molar mass is a constant property of a substance, the vapour density is independent of temperature and pressure. Statement (C) is incorrect.

Statement (D):
The vapour density of a gas with respect to hydrogen is given by:
$\text{Vapour density} = \dfrac{M_{\text{gas}}}{M_{\text{H}_2}} = \dfrac{M_{\text{gas}}}{2}$
$\Rightarrow M_{\text{gas}} = 2 \times \text{Vapour density}$
The molar mass of a gas is twice its vapour density with respect to hydrogen, not half. Statement (D) is incorrect.

Therefore, there are $2$ correct statements.

Answer: $2$

(Given atomic mass of $\text{O} = 16 \text{ u}$)
questions.question:
The density of a gas relative to oxygen gas ($\text{O}_2$) under identical conditions of temperature and pressure is $1.5$. The molar mass of the gas is:
(Given atomic mass of $\text{O} = 16 \text{ u}$)
questions.solution:
Using the ideal gas equation, the density of a gas is given by $d = \dfrac{PM}{RT}$, where $P$ is pressure, $M$ is molar mass, $R$ is the universal gas constant, and $T$ is temperature.

Under identical conditions of temperature and pressure, the density of a gas is directly proportional to its molar mass.

$\dfrac{d_{\text{gas}}}{d_{\text{O}_2}} = \dfrac{M_{\text{gas}}}{M_{\text{O}_2}}$

Given that the relative density of the gas with respect to oxygen is $1.5$, and the molar mass of $\text{O}_2$ is $2 \times 16 = 32 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$.

$1.5 = \dfrac{M_{\text{gas}}}{32}$

$M_{\text{gas}} = 1.5 \times 32 = 48 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$

Answer: $48 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$

(Given: $N_A = 6.0 \times 10^{23} \text{ mol}^{-1}$, atomic masses of C and O are $12 \text{ u}$ and $16 \text{ u}$ respectively)
questions.question:

(Given: $N_A = 6.0 \times 10^{23} \text{ mol}^{-1}$, atomic masses of C and O are $12 \text{ u}$ and $16 \text{ u}$ respectively)
questions.solution:
The mass of $6$ carbon atoms and $2$ oxygen atoms in a single molecule is:

$6 \times 12 + 2 \times 16 = 72 + 32 = 104 \text{ u}$

The mass of $1$ mole of these carbon and oxygen atoms is $104 \text{ g}$.

The mass of other elements in a single molecule is given as $3.0 \times 10^{-23} \text{ g}$.

The mass of these other elements in $1$ mole of the compound is:

$(3.0 \times 10^{-23} \text{ g}) \times (6.0 \times 10^{23} \text{ mol}^{-1}) = 18 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$

The total molar mass of the compound is the sum of the molar masses of all its constituent elements:

$\text{Molar mass} = 104 \text{ g mol}^{-1} + 18 \text{ g mol}^{-1} = 122 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$

Answer: $122 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$

questions.q: If the mass of a neutron is hypothetically doubled and the mass of a proton is halved, what will be the percentage change in the molar mass of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$? (Assume that $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ contains only $^1\text{H}$ and $^{16}\text{O}$ isotopes, and the mass of an electron is negligible)
questions.question: If the mass of a neutron is hypothetically doubled and the mass of a proton is halved, what will be the percentage change in the molar mass of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$? (Assume that $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ contains only $^1\text{H}$ and $^{16}\text{O}$ isotopes, and the mass of an electron is negligible)
questions.solution:
The molecule $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ consists of two $^1\text{H}$ atoms and one $^{16}\text{O}$ atom.

Number of protons in two $^1\text{H}$ atoms = $2 \times 1 = 2$
Number of neutrons in two $^1\text{H}$ atoms = $0$
Number of protons in one $^{16}\text{O}$ atom = $8$
Number of neutrons in one $^{16}\text{O}$ atom = $8$

Total number of protons in $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ = $2 + 8 = 10$
Total number of neutrons in $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ = $0 + 8 = 8$

Assuming the initial mass of a proton and a neutron to be approximately $1 \text{ amu}$ each, the initial molar mass of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ is:
$M_i = 10 \times 1 + 8 \times 1 = 18 \text{ amu}$

Given that the mass of a proton is halved and the mass of a neutron is doubled, the new masses are:
New mass of a proton = $0.5 \text{ amu}$
New mass of a neutron = $2 \text{ amu}$

The new molar mass of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ becomes:
$M_f = 10 \times 0.5 + 8 \times 2 = 5 + 16 = 21 \text{ amu}$

The percentage change in the molar mass is:
$\text{Percentage change} = \dfrac{M_f - M_i}{M_i} \times 100\%$

$\text{Percentage change} = \dfrac{21 - 18}{18} \times 100\% = \dfrac{3}{18} \times 100\% = \dfrac{100}{6}\% = 16.67\%$

Since the final mass is greater than the initial mass, it is an increase of $16.67\%$.

Answer: Increase by $16.67\%$

(B) $1.0\text{ g}$ of $\text{O}_3$ contains the maximum number of oxygen atoms because of its higher atomicity.
(C) $1.0\text{ g}$ of $\text{O}_2$ contains a greater number of molecules than $1.0\text{ g}$ of $\text{O}_3$.
(D) The ratio of the number of molecules in $1.0\text{ g}$ of $\text{O}_2$ to that in $1.0\text{ g}$ of $\text{O}_3$ is $2 : 3$.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
Number of moles of oxygen atoms in $1.0\text{ g}$ of $\text{O} = \dfrac{1.0}{16}$

Number of moles of oxygen atoms in $1.0\text{ g}$ of $\text{O}_2 = \dfrac{1.0}{32} \times 2 = \dfrac{1.0}{16}$

Number of moles of oxygen atoms in $1.0\text{ g}$ of $\text{O}_3 = \dfrac{1.0}{48} \times 3 = \dfrac{1.0}{16}$

Since the number of moles of oxygen atoms is the same in all three samples, they contain the same number of oxygen atoms. Thus, statement (A) is correct and (B) is incorrect.

Number of molecules in $1.0\text{ g}$ of $\text{O}_2 = \dfrac{1.0}{32} \times N_A$

Number of molecules in $1.0\text{ g}$ of $\text{O}_3 = \dfrac{1.0}{48} \times N_A$

Since $\dfrac{1}{32} > \dfrac{1}{48}$, $1.0\text{ g}$ of $\text{O}_2$ contains a greater number of molecules than $1.0\text{ g}$ of $\text{O}_3$. Thus, statement (C) is correct.

Ratio of the number of molecules in $1.0\text{ g}$ of $\text{O}_2$ to that in $1.0\text{ g}$ of $\text{O}_3 = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{32}}{\dfrac{1}{48}} = \dfrac{48}{32} = \dfrac{3}{2}$. Thus, statement (D) is incorrect.

Therefore, only statements (A) and (C) are correct.

Answer: (A) and (C) only

questions.q:
The total number of electrons present in $9.6 \text{ g}$ of sulphate ion ($\text{SO}_4^{2-}$) is:
(Given: Atomic numbers of S and O are $16$ and $8$ respectively, and their atomic masses are $32$ and $16$ respectively; $N_A$ is the Avogadro constant)
questions.question:
The total number of electrons present in $9.6 \text{ g}$ of sulphate ion ($\text{SO}_4^{2-}$) is:
(Given: Atomic numbers of S and O are $16$ and $8$ respectively, and their atomic masses are $32$ and $16$ respectively; $N_A$ is the Avogadro constant)
questions.solution:
The molar mass of sulphate ion ($\text{SO}_4^{2-}$) is calculated as:

Molar mass $= 32 + 4 \times 16 = 96 \text{ g/mol}$

The number of moles of $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ in $9.6 \text{ g}$ is:

Number of moles $= \dfrac{9.6}{96} = 0.1 \text{ mol}$

The number of electrons in one $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ ion is the sum of the electrons in one sulphur atom, four oxygen atoms, and the two extra electrons from the negative charge:

Number of electrons $= 16 + (4 \times 8) + 2 = 16 + 32 + 2 = 50$

The total number of electrons in $0.1 \text{ mol}$ of $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ is:

Total electrons $= 0.1 \times 50 \times N_A = 5.0 N_A$

Answer: $5.0 N_A$

(Given: Atomic masses $\text{K} = 39\text{ u}$, $\text{I} = 127\text{ u}$; $N_A = 6.02 \times 10^{23}\text{ mol}^{-1}$)

Volume $= \dfrac{\text{Mass}}{\text{Density}} = \dfrac{117}{0.78} = 150 \text{ mL}$

Number of water molecules $= \dfrac{1}{120} \times 6.0 \times 10^{23} = 5.0 \times 10^{21}$

Answer: $5.0 \times 10^{21}$

questions.question: A mixture containing only two pure substances, P and Q, has a total mass of $24.4\text{ g}$ and contains a total of $0.50\text{ mol}$ of particles. If the molar mass of Q is $44\text{ g mol}^{-1}$ and the mixture contains $0.20\text{ mol}$ of P, the molar mass of P is:
questions.solution:
Total moles of particles in the mixture $= 0.50\text{ mol}$

Moles of P, $n_P = 0.20\text{ mol}$

Moles of Q, $n_Q = 0.50 - 0.20 = 0.30\text{ mol}$

Mass of Q, $m_Q = n_Q \times M_Q = 0.30 \times 44 = 13.2\text{ g}$

Total mass of the mixture $= 24.4\text{ g}$

Mass of P, $m_P = 24.4 - 13.2 = 11.2\text{ g}$

Molar mass of P, $M_P = \dfrac{m_P}{n_P} = \dfrac{11.2}{0.20} = 56\text{ g mol}^{-1}$

Answer: $56\text{ g mol}^{-1}$
questions.explanation:

Moles of P, $n_P = 0.20\text{ mol}$

Mass of P, $m_P = 24.4 - 13.2 = 11.2\text{ g}$

Molar mass of P, $M_P = \dfrac{m_P}{n_P} = \dfrac{11.2}{0.20} = 56\text{ g mol}^{-1}$

Answer: $56\text{ g mol}^{-1}$

questions.solution:
The chemical equation for the formation of chlorine gas from chlorine atoms is:

$2\text{Cl} \rightarrow \text{Cl}_2$

From the stoichiometry of the reaction, $2$ moles of $\text{Cl}$ atoms produce $1$ mole of $\text{Cl}_2$ gas.

Moles of $\text{Cl}_2$ gas formed from $6$ moles of $\text{Cl}$ atoms = $\dfrac{6}{2} = 3\text{ moles}$

Given the molar volume of an ideal gas at STP ($273\text{ K}$ and $1\text{ bar}$) is $22.7\text{ L mol}^{-1}$.

Volume occupied by the $\text{Cl}_2$ gas = $3\text{ moles} \times 22.7\text{ L mol}^{-1} = 68.1\text{ L}$

Answer: $68.1\text{ L}$

questions.solution:

questions.q:
One molecule of haemoglobin binds with four molecules of oxygen. If $1.7 \text{ g}$ of haemoglobin combines completely with $2.463 \text{ mL}$ of oxygen gas at $300 \text{ K}$ and $1 \text{ atm}$ pressure, the molar mass of haemoglobin is $x \times 10^3 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$. The value of $x$ is ____.
(Given: $R = 0.0821 \text{ L atm K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}$)
questions.question:
One molecule of haemoglobin binds with four molecules of oxygen. If $1.7 \text{ g}$ of haemoglobin combines completely with $2.463 \text{ mL}$ of oxygen gas at $300 \text{ K}$ and $1 \text{ atm}$ pressure, the molar mass of haemoglobin is $x \times 10^3 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$. The value of $x$ is ____.
(Given: $R = 0.0821 \text{ L atm K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}$)
questions.solution:
Using the ideal gas equation, the number of moles of oxygen gas is calculated as:

$n_{O_2} = \dfrac{PV}{RT}$

$n_{O_2} = \dfrac{1 \times 2.463 \times 10^{-3}}{0.0821 \times 300}$

$n_{O_2} = \dfrac{2.463 \times 10^{-3}}{24.63} = 10^{-4} \text{ mol}$

Since one molecule of haemoglobin binds with four molecules of oxygen, the number of moles of haemoglobin is:

$n_{Hb} = \dfrac{n_{O_2}}{4} = \dfrac{10^{-4}}{4} = 2.5 \times 10^{-5} \text{ mol}$

The molar mass of haemoglobin is given by the ratio of its mass to the number of moles:

$M_{Hb} = \dfrac{W_{Hb}}{n_{Hb}}$

$M_{Hb} = \dfrac{1.7}{2.5 \times 10^{-5}} = 68000 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$

$M_{Hb} = 68 \times 10^3 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$

Comparing this with $x \times 10^3 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$, we get $x = 68$.

Answer: $68$

Number of moles of lithium $= \dfrac{7.7 \times 10^{12}\text{ g}}{7\text{ g mol}^{-1}} = 1.1 \times 10^{12}\text{ mol}$

Answer: $1.1 \times 10^{12}$

Consider the following statements regarding the volumes of gases under identical conditions of temperature and pressure, assuming ideal behaviour:
(A) For equal masses of $\text{O}_2$ and $\text{SO}_2$, the ratio of their volumes is $2 : 1$.
(B) For equal masses of $\text{He}$ and $\text{CH}_4$, the ratio of their volumes is $1 : 4$.
(C) For equal masses of $\text{H}_2$, $\text{CH}_4$ and $\text{SO}_2$, the ratio of their volumes is $32 : 4 : 1$.
(D) For equal masses of $\text{N}_2$ and $\text{CO}$, the ratio of their volumes is $1 : 1$.

[Given atomic masses (in $\text{g mol}^{-1}$): $\text{H} = 1, \text{He} = 4, \text{C} = 12, \text{N} = 14, \text{O} = 16, \text{S} = 32$]

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.question:

(A) For equal masses of $\text{O}_2$ and $\text{SO}_2$, the ratio of their volumes is $2 : 1$.
(B) For equal masses of $\text{He}$ and $\text{CH}_4$, the ratio of their volumes is $1 : 4$.
(C) For equal masses of $\text{H}_2$, $\text{CH}_4$ and $\text{SO}_2$, the ratio of their volumes is $32 : 4 : 1$.
(D) For equal masses of $\text{N}_2$ and $\text{CO}$, the ratio of their volumes is $1 : 1$.

[Given atomic masses (in $\text{g mol}^{-1}$): $\text{H} = 1, \text{He} = 4, \text{C} = 12, \text{N} = 14, \text{O} = 16, \text{S} = 32$]

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
According to Avogadro's law, under identical conditions of temperature and pressure, the volume of a gas is directly proportional to its number of moles ($V \propto n$).

For a given mass $w$, the number of moles is $n = \dfrac{w}{M}$, where $M$ is the molar mass.

(A) Molar masses of $\text{O}_2$ and $\text{SO}_2$ are $32 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$ and $64 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$ respectively.
$V_{\text{O}_2} : V_{\text{SO}_2} = \dfrac{w}{32} : \dfrac{w}{64} = 2 : 1$. Statement (A) is correct.

(B) Molar masses of $\text{He}$ and $\text{CH}_4$ are $4 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$ and $16 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$ respectively.
$V_{\text{He}} : V_{\text{CH}_4} = \dfrac{w}{4} : \dfrac{w}{16} = 4 : 1$. Statement (B) is incorrect.

(C) Molar masses of $\text{H}_2$, $\text{CH}_4$ and $\text{SO}_2$ are $2 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$, $16 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$ and $64 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$ respectively.
$V_{\text{H}_2} : V_{\text{CH}_4} : V_{\text{SO}_2} = \dfrac{w}{2} : \dfrac{w}{16} : \dfrac{w}{64} = 32 : 4 : 1$. Statement (C) is correct.

(D) Molar masses of $\text{N}_2$ and $\text{CO}$ are $28 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$ and $28 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$ respectively.
$V_{\text{N}_2} : V_{\text{CO}} = \dfrac{w}{28} : \dfrac{w}{28} = 1 : 1$. Statement (D) is correct.

Thus, statements (A), (C) and (D) are correct.

Answer: (A), (C) and (D) only

A rigid container of constant volume is filled with oxygen gas ($\text{O}_2$) at $298\text{ K}$ and $1\text{ atm}$, and the mass of the gas is found to be $m_{\text{O}_2}$. The container is then completely evacuated and filled with sulphur dioxide gas ($\text{SO}_2$) at the same temperature and pressure. If the mass of the sulphur dioxide gas is $m_{\text{SO}_2}$, which of the following relationships is correct?
(Assume ideal gas behaviour)
questions.question:
A rigid container of constant volume is filled with oxygen gas ($\text{O}_2$) at $298\text{ K}$ and $1\text{ atm}$, and the mass of the gas is found to be $m_{\text{O}_2}$. The container is then completely evacuated and filled with sulphur dioxide gas ($\text{SO}_2$) at the same temperature and pressure. If the mass of the sulphur dioxide gas is $m_{\text{SO}_2}$, which of the following relationships is correct?
(Assume ideal gas behaviour)
questions.solution:
Using the ideal gas equation $PV = nRT$

Since the volume $V$, pressure $P$, and temperature $T$ are constant for both gases, the number of moles $n$ must be equal.

$n_{\text{O}_2} = n_{\text{SO}_2}$

The number of moles is given by the ratio of mass to molar mass $n = \dfrac{m}{M}$

Molar mass of $\text{O}_2 = 32 \text{ g/mol}$

Molar mass of $\text{SO}_2 = 64 \text{ g/mol}$

Substituting the values:

$\dfrac{m_{\text{O}_2}}{32} = \dfrac{m_{\text{SO}_2}}{64}$

$m_{\text{O}_2} = \dfrac{32}{64} m_{\text{SO}_2}$

$m_{\text{O}_2} = \dfrac{1}{2} m_{\text{SO}_2}$

Answer: $m_{\text{O}_2} = \dfrac{1}{2} m_{\text{SO}_2}$

Consider the following statements regarding dry air and moist air:
(A) The average molar mass of dry air is greater than that of moist air.
(B) At identical conditions of temperature and pressure, dry air is denser than moist air.
(C) The molar mass of water vapour is higher than the average molar mass of dry air.
(D) The vapour density of moist air is greater than that of dry air.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding dry air and moist air:
(A) The average molar mass of dry air is greater than that of moist air.
(B) At identical conditions of temperature and pressure, dry air is denser than moist air.
(C) The molar mass of water vapour is higher than the average molar mass of dry air.
(D) The vapour density of moist air is greater than that of dry air.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
Dry air is primarily composed of nitrogen ($N_2$, molar mass $28 \text{ g/mol}$) and oxygen ($O_2$, molar mass $32 \text{ g/mol}$). The average molar mass of dry air is approximately $28.96 \text{ g/mol}$.

Moist air contains water vapour ($H_2O$), which has a molar mass of $18 \text{ g/mol}$.

Since the molar mass of water vapour is less than the average molar mass of dry air, the addition of water vapour decreases the overall average molar mass of the mixture. Thus, the average molar mass of dry air is greater than that of moist air. Statement (A) is correct.

From the ideal gas equation, density is given by $\rho = \dfrac{PM}{RT}$. At identical temperature and pressure, density is directly proportional to the average molar mass. Since dry air has a higher average molar mass, it is denser than moist air. Statement (B) is correct.

The molar mass of water vapour ($18 \text{ g/mol}$) is lower than the average molar mass of dry air ($28.96 \text{ g/mol}$). Statement (C) is incorrect.

Vapour density is half of the average molar mass. Since moist air has a lower average molar mass than dry air, its vapour density is also lower. Statement (D) is incorrect.

Therefore, only statements (A) and (B) are correct.

Answer: (A) and (B) only

Due to strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding, hydrogen fluoride ($\text{HF}$) undergoes association in the vapour phase. At a particular temperature and pressure, the apparent molar mass of $\text{HF}$ vapour is experimentally determined to be $48\text{ g mol}^{-1}$. Which of the following pairs of species could constitute this vapour?
(Given: Atomic masses $\text{H} = 1$, $\text{F} = 19$ in $\text{u}$)
questions.question:
Due to strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding, hydrogen fluoride ($\text{HF}$) undergoes association in the vapour phase. At a particular temperature and pressure, the apparent molar mass of $\text{HF}$ vapour is experimentally determined to be $48\text{ g mol}^{-1}$. Which of the following pairs of species could constitute this vapour?
(Given: Atomic masses $\text{H} = 1$, $\text{F} = 19$ in $\text{u}$)
questions.solution:
The molar mass of a single $\text{HF}$ molecule is $1 + 19 = 20 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$.

The apparent molar mass of a gaseous mixture is the weighted average of the molar masses of its constituent species. Therefore, the apparent molar mass must lie strictly between the molar masses of the individual components present in the mixture.

Let us calculate the molar masses of the various associated species of $\text{HF}$:
$\text{HF} = 20 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$
$(\text{HF})_2 = 2 \times 20 = 40 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$
$(\text{HF})_3 = 3 \times 20 = 60 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$
$(\text{HF})_4 = 4 \times 20 = 80 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$
$(\text{HF})_5 = 5 \times 20 = 100 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$

The experimentally determined apparent molar mass is $48 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$.

Checking the given options:
For $(\text{HF})_3$ and $(\text{HF})_4$, the molar masses are $60$ and $80$. $48$ does not lie between them.
For $\text{HF}$ and $(\text{HF})_2$, the molar masses are $20$ and $40$. $48$ does not lie between them.
For $(\text{HF})_2$ and $(\text{HF})_3$, the molar masses are $40$ and $60$. $48$ lies exactly between $40$ and $60$.
For $(\text{HF})_4$ and $(\text{HF})_5$, the molar masses are $80$ and $100$. $48$ does not lie between them.

Thus, the vapour could constitute $(\text{HF})_2$ and $(\text{HF})_3$.

Answer: $(\text{HF})_2$ and $(\text{HF})_3$

GasPercentage by volume (%)Molar mass ($\text{g mol}^{-1}$)
$\text{Ar}$3040

If the average molar mass of the gaseous mixture is $34.4 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$, the molar mass of gas $X$ is:
questions.solution:
For a gaseous mixture, the volume percentage is equal to the mole percentage.

Let the total number of moles of the mixture be $100$.

Number of moles of $\text{Ar}$, $n_{\text{Ar}} = 30$
Number of moles of $X$, $n_X = 70$

The average molar mass of the mixture is given by:
$M_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{n_{\text{Ar}} M_{\text{Ar}} + n_X M_X}{n_{\text{Ar}} + n_X}$

Substituting the given values:
$34.4 = \dfrac{30 \times 40 + 70 \times M_X}{100}$

$3440 = 1200 + 70 M_X$

$70 M_X = 3440 - 1200$

$70 M_X = 2240$

$M_X = \dfrac{2240}{70} = 32 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$

Answer: $32$

(Given: Molar masses of $\text{H}$ and $\text{He}$ are $1 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$ and $4 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$ respectively)
questions.question:
An interstellar gas cloud is composed of $90\%$ hydrogen ($\text{H}_2$) and $10\%$ helium ($\text{He}$) by mass. The average molar mass of this gas mixture is closest to:

(Given: Molar masses of $\text{H}$ and $\text{He}$ are $1 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$ and $4 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$ respectively)
questions.solution:
Let the total mass of the gas mixture be $100 \text{ g}$.

Mass of $\text{H}_2 = 90 \text{ g}$

Mass of $\text{He} = 10 \text{ g}$

Molar mass of $\text{H}_2 = 2 \times 1 = 2 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$

Molar mass of $\text{He} = 4 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$

Number of moles of $\text{H}_2 = \dfrac{90}{2} = 45 \text{ mol}$

Number of moles of $\text{He} = \dfrac{10}{4} = 2.5 \text{ mol}$

Total number of moles $= 45 + 2.5 = 47.5 \text{ mol}$

Average molar mass $= \dfrac{\text{Total mass}}{\text{Total moles}} = \dfrac{100}{47.5} = \dfrac{40}{19} \approx 2.11 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$

Answer: $2.11 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$

A $16\text{ g}$ mixture of $\text{SO}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$ occupies a volume of $8.96\text{ L}$ at $273\text{ K}$ and $1\text{ atm}$. The percentage of $\text{O}_2$ by mass in the mixture is
(Given: Molar volume of a gas at $273\text{ K}$ and $1\text{ atm}$ is $22.4\text{ L mol}^{-1}$)
questions.question:
A $16\text{ g}$ mixture of $\text{SO}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$ occupies a volume of $8.96\text{ L}$ at $273\text{ K}$ and $1\text{ atm}$. The percentage of $\text{O}_2$ by mass in the mixture is
(Given: Molar volume of a gas at $273\text{ K}$ and $1\text{ atm}$ is $22.4\text{ L mol}^{-1}$)
questions.solution:
Total number of moles of the mixture is given by $n = \dfrac{V}{V_m} = \dfrac{8.96}{22.4} = 0.4 \text{ mol}$

Let the mass of $\text{O}_2$ in the mixture be $x \text{ g}$.

The mass of $\text{SO}_2$ will be $(16 - x) \text{ g}$.

Molar mass of $\text{O}_2 = 32 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$ and $\text{SO}_2 = 64 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$.

The total number of moles is the sum of moles of $\text{O}_2$ and $\text{SO}_2$:

$\dfrac{x}{32} + \dfrac{16 - x}{64} = 0.4$

Multiplying by $64$, we get:

$2x + 16 - x = 25.6$

$x = 9.6 \text{ g}$

The percentage of $\text{O}_2$ by mass is $\dfrac{9.6}{16} \times 100 = 60\%$

Answer: $60\%$

A gaseous mixture contains equal masses of $\text{SO}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$. The density of this gas mixture at $273\text{ K}$ and $1\text{ atm}$ is closest to:
(Given: Molar volume of an ideal gas at $273\text{ K}$ and $1\text{ atm}$ is $22.4\text{ L mol}^{-1}$; atomic masses: $\text{S} = 32$, $\text{O} = 16$)
questions.question:
A gaseous mixture contains equal masses of $\text{SO}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$. The density of this gas mixture at $273\text{ K}$ and $1\text{ atm}$ is closest to:
(Given: Molar volume of an ideal gas at $273\text{ K}$ and $1\text{ atm}$ is $22.4\text{ L mol}^{-1}$; atomic masses: $\text{S} = 32$, $\text{O} = 16$)
questions.solution:
Let the mass of $\text{SO}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$ in the mixture be $w$ each.

Molar mass of $\text{SO}_2 = 64\text{ g mol}^{-1}$
Molar mass of $\text{O}_2 = 32\text{ g mol}^{-1}$

Total mass of the mixture $= w + w = 2w$

Total number of moles $= \dfrac{w}{64} + \dfrac{w}{32} = \dfrac{3w}{64}$

Average molar mass of the mixture, $M_{\text{mix}} = \dfrac{\text{Total mass}}{\text{Total moles}} = \dfrac{2w}{\dfrac{3w}{64}} = \dfrac{128}{3}\text{ g mol}^{-1}$

Density of the mixture, $d = \dfrac{PM_{\text{mix}}}{RT}$

Since the molar volume $\dfrac{RT}{P} = 22.4\text{ L mol}^{-1}$ at $273\text{ K}$ and $1\text{ atm}$,

$d = \dfrac{M_{\text{mix}}}{22.4} = \dfrac{128}{3 \times 22.4} = \dfrac{128}{67.2} \approx 1.90\text{ g L}^{-1}$

Answer: $1.90\text{ g L}^{-1}$

questions.question:

(Given : $R = 0.0821\text{ L atm K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$, atomic masses : $\text{Ar} = 40\text{ u}, \text{N} = 14\text{ u}$)

Using the ideal gas equation, $PV = n_{total}RT$

$n_{total} = \dfrac{PV}{RT} = \dfrac{1.5 \times 16.42}{0.0821 \times 300}$

(Given atomic masses in $\text{u}$: $\text{N} = 14$, $\text{O} = 16$)
questions.question:
A sample of $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4$ gas is heated in a closed vessel and is found to be $15\%$ dissociated into $\text{NO}_2$ gas. The average molar mass of the resulting gas mixture in $\text{g mol}^{-1}$ is:
(Given atomic masses in $\text{u}$: $\text{N} = 14$, $\text{O} = 16$)
questions.solution:
The dissociation reaction is given by:

$\text{N}_2\text{O}_4(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NO}_2(g)$

Let the initial moles of $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4$ be $1$.
Moles at equilibrium:
$\text{N}_2\text{O}_4 = 1 - \alpha$
$\text{NO}_2 = 2\alpha$

Total moles at equilibrium $= 1 - \alpha + 2\alpha = 1 + \alpha$

Given the degree of dissociation $\alpha = 15\% = 0.15$
Total moles $= 1 + 0.15 = 1.15$

Molar mass of $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4 = 2 \times 14 + 4 \times 16 = 92 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$

Since the total mass of the mixture remains conserved, the average molar mass $M_{avg}$ is:

$M_{avg} = \dfrac{\text{Total mass}}{\text{Total moles}} = \dfrac{92}{1 + \alpha}$

$M_{avg} = \dfrac{92}{1.15} = 80 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$

Answer: $80$

questions.solution:
The observed vapour density $d$ is related to the theoretical vapour density $D$ by the formula:

(D) matches with (III).

questions.solution:
The molecular formula of ibuprofen is $\text{C}_{13}\text{H}_{18}\text{O}_2$.

Number of moles of hydrogen in the sample = $\dfrac{18}{13} \times 0.26 = 0.36 \text{ mol}$.

Mass of hydrogen = $0.36 \times 1 = 0.36 \text{ g}$.

Answer: $0.36\text{ g}$

questions.q: Analysis shows that a non-stoichiometric sample of wustite has the empirical formula $\text{Fe}_{0.95}\text{O}$. The fraction of the total iron present as $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ ions in this sample is:
questions.question: Analysis shows that a non-stoichiometric sample of wustite has the empirical formula $\text{Fe}_{0.95}\text{O}$. The fraction of the total iron present as $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ ions in this sample is:
questions.solution:
Let the formula of the sample be written as $\text{Fe}_{95}\text{O}_{100}$.

Let the number of $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ ions be $x$.

The number of $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ ions is $95 - x$.

To maintain electrical neutrality, the total positive charge on iron ions must equal the total negative charge on oxygen ions.

$3x + 2(95 - x) = 100 \times 2$

$3x + 190 - 2x = 200$

$x = 10$

The fraction of total iron present as $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ ions is $\dfrac{10}{95} = \dfrac{2}{19}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{2}{19}$

Number of carbon atoms per molecule $= 24$

$\dfrac{288}{M} = \dfrac{3}{4}$

$M = \dfrac{288 \times 4}{3} = 96 \times 4 = 384\text{ g mol}^{-1}$

Answer: $384\text{ g mol}^{-1}$

A polystyrene sample was prepared by heating styrene with a brominated initiator, resulting in a polymer with the formula $\text{C}_6\text{HBr}_4(\text{C}_8\text{H}_8)_n$. If the polymer contains $10.0\%$ bromine by mass, the value of $n$ is ____. (Nearest integer)
(Given atomic masses: $\text{C} = 12$, $\text{H} = 1$, $\text{Br} = 80\text{ u}$)
questions.question:
A polystyrene sample was prepared by heating styrene with a brominated initiator, resulting in a polymer with the formula $\text{C}_6\text{HBr}_4(\text{C}_8\text{H}_8)_n$. If the polymer contains $10.0\%$ bromine by mass, the value of $n$ is ____. (Nearest integer)
(Given atomic masses: $\text{C} = 12$, $\text{H} = 1$, $\text{Br} = 80\text{ u}$)
questions.solution:
The molecular formula of the polymer is given as $\text{C}_6\text{HBr}_4(\text{C}_8\text{H}_8)_n$.

Mass of bromine in one mole of the polymer = $4 \times 80 = 320 \text{ g}$

Molar mass of the initiator fragment $\text{C}_6\text{HBr}_4$ = $(6 \times 12) + (1 \times 1) + (4 \times 80) = 72 + 1 + 320 = 393 \text{ g/mol}$

Molar mass of the repeating unit $\text{C}_8\text{H}_8$ = $(8 \times 12) + (8 \times 1) = 96 + 8 = 104 \text{ g/mol}$

Total molar mass of the polymer = $393 + 104n$

Given that the polymer contains $10.0\%$ bromine by mass:

$\dfrac{320}{393 + 104n} \times 100 = 10$

$\dfrac{3200}{393 + 104n} = 1$

$393 + 104n = 3200$

$104n = 3200 - 393$

$104n = 2807$

$n = \dfrac{2807}{104} \approx 26.99$

Rounding to the nearest integer, we get $n = 27$.

Answer: $27$

A certain mass of a gaseous hydrocarbon having the empirical formula $\text{CH}_2$ occupies exactly one-third of the volume occupied by the same mass of nitrogen gas under identical conditions of temperature and pressure. The molecular formula of the hydrocarbon is:
(Given atomic masses in $\text{u}$: $\text{H} = 1$, $\text{C} = 12$, $\text{N} = 14$)
questions.question:
A certain mass of a gaseous hydrocarbon having the empirical formula $\text{CH}_2$ occupies exactly one-third of the volume occupied by the same mass of nitrogen gas under identical conditions of temperature and pressure. The molecular formula of the hydrocarbon is:
(Given atomic masses in $\text{u}$: $\text{H} = 1$, $\text{C} = 12$, $\text{N} = 14$)
questions.solution:
Let the mass of the hydrocarbon and nitrogen gas be $m$.

Molar mass of $\text{N}_2 = 28 \text{ g/mol}$.

Number of moles of $\text{N}_2$, $n_{\text{N}_2} = \dfrac{m}{28}$.

Number of moles of the hydrocarbon, $n_{\text{HC}} = \dfrac{m}{M_{\text{HC}}}$.

According to Avogadro's law, at constant temperature and pressure, volume is directly proportional to the number of moles ($V \propto n$).

Given $V_{\text{HC}} = \dfrac{1}{3} V_{\text{N}_2}$, which implies $n_{\text{HC}} = \dfrac{1}{3} n_{\text{N}_2}$.

$\dfrac{m}{M_{\text{HC}}} = \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{m}{28}$

$M_{\text{HC}} = 3 \times 28 = 84 \text{ g/mol}$.

The empirical formula of the hydrocarbon is $\text{CH}_2$.

Empirical formula mass $= 12 + 2(1) = 14 \text{ u}$.

Let the molecular formula be $(\text{CH}_2)_n$.

$n = \dfrac{\text{Molecular mass}}{\text{Empirical formula mass}} = \dfrac{84}{14} = 6$

The molecular formula of the hydrocarbon is $(\text{CH}_2)_6 = \text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}$.

Answer: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}$

$n = \dfrac{\text{Molar mass}}{\text{Empirical formula mass}} = \dfrac{60}{30} = 2$.

The molecular formula is $(\text{CH}_2\text{O})_n = (\text{CH}_2\text{O})_2 = \text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}_2$.

questions.question: A compound contains two elements, X and Y. The ratio of the mass of X to the mass of Y in the compound is $3:4$. If the ratio of the atomic masses of X and Y is $1:2$, the empirical formula of the compound is:

The empirical formula of the compound is $X_3Y_2$.

questions.q: A compound contains equal masses of three elements $X$, $Y$ and $Z$. If the atomic masses of $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ are $16$, $24$ and $32$ respectively, the empirical formula of the compound is
questions.question: A compound contains equal masses of three elements $X$, $Y$ and $Z$. If the atomic masses of $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ are $16$, $24$ and $32$ respectively, the empirical formula of the compound is
questions.solution:
Let the mass of each element $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ present in the compound be $m$.

The number of moles of each element is given by the ratio of its mass to its atomic mass.

Moles of $X = \dfrac{m}{16}$

Moles of $Y = \dfrac{m}{24}$

Moles of $Z = \dfrac{m}{32}$

The molar ratio of the elements $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ is:

$n_X : n_Y : n_Z = \dfrac{m}{16} : \dfrac{m}{24} : \dfrac{m}{32}$

Dividing by $m$ and multiplying by the least common multiple of $16$, $24$, and $32$, which is $96$, we get:

$n_X : n_Y : n_Z = \left(\dfrac{1}{16} \times 96\right) : \left(\dfrac{1}{24} \times 96\right) : \left(\dfrac{1}{32} \times 96\right)$

$n_X : n_Y : n_Z = 6 : 4 : 3$

The simplest whole number ratio of the atoms is $6 : 4 : 3$.

The empirical formula of the compound is $X_6Y_4Z_3$.

Answer: $X_6Y_4Z_3$

Dividing by $m$ and multiplying by the least common multiple of $16$, $24$, and $32$, which is $96$, we get:

$n_X : n_Y : n_Z = \left(\dfrac{1}{16} \times 96\right) : \left(\dfrac{1}{24} \times 96\right) : \left(\dfrac{1}{32} \times 96\right)$

$n_X : n_Y : n_Z = 6 : 4 : 3$

The simplest whole number ratio of the atoms is $6 : 4 : 3$.

The empirical formula of the compound is $X_6Y_4Z_3$.

Answer: $X_6Y_4Z_3$

questions.q:
A gaseous oxide of nitrogen contains $46.67\%$ nitrogen by mass. If one molecule of the oxide contains exactly one nitrogen atom, the density of this oxide relative to oxygen gas ($\text{O}_2$) under identical conditions is closest to:
(Given atomic masses: $\text{N} = 14 \text{ u}$, $\text{O} = 16 \text{ u}$)
questions.question:
A gaseous oxide of nitrogen contains $46.67\%$ nitrogen by mass. If one molecule of the oxide contains exactly one nitrogen atom, the density of this oxide relative to oxygen gas ($\text{O}_2$) under identical conditions is closest to:
(Given atomic masses: $\text{N} = 14 \text{ u}$, $\text{O} = 16 \text{ u}$)
questions.solution:
Let the molar mass of the gaseous oxide be $M$.

Since one molecule of the oxide contains exactly one nitrogen atom, one mole of the oxide contains $14 \text{ g}$ of nitrogen.

The mass percentage of nitrogen is given as $46.67\%$.

$\dfrac{14}{M} \times 100 = 46.67$

$M = \dfrac{1400}{46.67} \approx 30 \text{ g/mol}$

The molar mass of oxygen gas ($\text{O}_2$) is $32 \text{ g/mol}$.

Under identical conditions of temperature and pressure, the density of a gas is directly proportional to its molar mass ($d = \dfrac{PM}{RT}$).

Relative density = $\dfrac{M_{\text{oxide}}}{M_{\text{O}_2}} = \dfrac{30}{32} = 0.9375$

The closest value is $0.94$.

Answer: $0.94$

questions.q: A metal $M$ forms two oxides, $X$ and $Y$. It is observed that $1.00\text{ g}$ of metal $M$ combines with $0.27\text{ g}$ of oxygen to form oxide $X$, while $1.00\text{ g}$ of the same metal combines with $0.405\text{ g}$ of oxygen to form oxide $Y$. If the empirical formula of oxide $X$ is $MO$, the empirical formula of oxide $Y$ is:
questions.question: A metal $M$ forms two oxides, $X$ and $Y$. It is observed that $1.00\text{ g}$ of metal $M$ combines with $0.27\text{ g}$ of oxygen to form oxide $X$, while $1.00\text{ g}$ of the same metal combines with $0.405\text{ g}$ of oxygen to form oxide $Y$. If the empirical formula of oxide $X$ is $MO$, the empirical formula of oxide $Y$ is:
questions.solution:
For a fixed mass of metal $M$, the ratio of the masses of oxygen in oxides $X$ and $Y$ is $0.27 : 0.405$.

Simplifying this ratio gives $270 : 405 = 2 : 3$.

Since the empirical formula of oxide $X$ is $MO$, there is $1$ atom of oxygen per atom of metal $M$.

Therefore, in oxide $Y$, the number of oxygen atoms per atom of metal $M$ is $\dfrac{3}{2} \times 1 = 1.5$.

The ratio of $M$ to $O$ in oxide $Y$ is $1 : 1.5$, which simplifies to $2 : 3$.

Thus, the empirical formula of oxide $Y$ is $M_2O_3$.

Answer: $M_2O_3$

When a sample of heptane ($\text{C}_7\text{H}_{16}$) is completely burnt in an excess of oxygen, $15.4\text{ g}$ of $\text{CO}_2$ is produced. The mass of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ formed simultaneously is:
(Given molar masses in $\text{g mol}^{-1}$: $\text{C} = 12$, $\text{H} = 1$, $\text{O} = 16$)
questions.question:
When a sample of heptane ($\text{C}_7\text{H}_{16}$) is completely burnt in an excess of oxygen, $15.4\text{ g}$ of $\text{CO}_2$ is produced. The mass of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ formed simultaneously is:
(Given molar masses in $\text{g mol}^{-1}$: $\text{C} = 12$, $\text{H} = 1$, $\text{O} = 16$)
questions.solution:
The balanced chemical equation for the combustion of heptane is:

$\text{C}_7\text{H}_{16} + 11\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 7\text{CO}_2 + 8\text{H}_2\text{O}$

Molar mass of $\text{CO}_2 = 44\text{ g mol}^{-1}$
Molar mass of $\text{H}_2\text{O} = 18\text{ g mol}^{-1}$

Moles of $\text{CO}_2$ produced = $\dfrac{15.4}{44} = 0.35\text{ mol}$

From the balanced equation, $7\text{ moles}$ of $\text{CO}_2$ are produced along with $8\text{ moles}$ of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$.

Moles of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ produced = $\dfrac{8}{7} \times 0.35 = 0.40\text{ mol}$

Mass of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ produced = $0.40 \times 18 = 7.2\text{ g}$

Answer: $7.2\text{ g}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
A rocket is fuelled with liquid decane ($\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{22}$) and liquid oxygen. What mass of oxygen is required to completely combust $1.0\text{ L}$ of decane?
(Given: Density of decane $= 0.710\text{ g mL}^{-1}$, Molar masses in $\text{g mol}^{-1}$: $\text{C} = 12$, $\text{H} = 1$, $\text{O} = 16$)
questions.question:
A rocket is fuelled with liquid decane ($\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{22}$) and liquid oxygen. What mass of oxygen is required to completely combust $1.0\text{ L}$ of decane?
(Given: Density of decane $= 0.710\text{ g mL}^{-1}$, Molar masses in $\text{g mol}^{-1}$: $\text{C} = 12$, $\text{H} = 1$, $\text{O} = 16$)
questions.solution:
Volume of decane = $1.0\text{ L} = 1000\text{ mL}$

Mass of decane = $1000\text{ mL} \times 0.710\text{ g mL}^{-1} = 710\text{ g}$

Molar mass of decane ($\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{22}$) = $10 \times 12 + 22 \times 1 = 142\text{ g mol}^{-1}$

Moles of decane = $\dfrac{710}{142} = 5\text{ mol}$

The balanced chemical equation for the combustion of decane is:

$\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{22} + \dfrac{31}{2}\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 10\text{CO}_2 + 11\text{H}_2\text{O}$

From the stoichiometry, $1\text{ mol}$ of decane requires $\dfrac{31}{2} = 15.5\text{ mol}$ of $\text{O}_2$.

Moles of $\text{O}_2$ required for $5\text{ mol}$ of decane = $5 \times 15.5 = 77.5\text{ mol}$

Mass of $\text{O}_2$ required = $77.5\text{ mol} \times 32\text{ g mol}^{-1} = 2480\text{ g} = 2.48\text{ kg}$

Answer: $2.48\text{ kg}$

questions.q:
Air contains $20\%$ $\text{O}_2$ by volume. What volume of air in litres is required at STP ($273\text{ K}$ and $1\text{ atm}$, molar volume $= 22.4\text{ L}$) for the complete combustion of $22\text{ g}$ of propane ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_8$)?
(Given atomic masses: $\text{C} = 12\text{ u}$, $\text{H} = 1\text{ u}$)
questions.question:
Air contains $20\%$ $\text{O}_2$ by volume. What volume of air in litres is required at STP ($273\text{ K}$ and $1\text{ atm}$, molar volume $= 22.4\text{ L}$) for the complete combustion of $22\text{ g}$ of propane ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_8$)?
(Given atomic masses: $\text{C} = 12\text{ u}$, $\text{H} = 1\text{ u}$)
questions.solution:
The balanced chemical equation for the combustion of propane is:

$\text{C}_3\text{H}_8 + 5\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 3\text{CO}_2 + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}$

Molar mass of propane ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_8$) $= 3 \times 12 + 8 \times 1 = 44\text{ g mol}^{-1}$

Moles of propane given $= \dfrac{22}{44} = 0.5\text{ mol}$

From the balanced equation, $1\text{ mol}$ of propane requires $5\text{ mol}$ of $\text{O}_2$.

Moles of $\text{O}_2$ required $= 0.5 \times 5 = 2.5\text{ mol}$

Volume of $\text{O}_2$ required at STP $= 2.5 \times 22.4\text{ L} = 56\text{ L}$

Since air contains $20\%$ $\text{O}_2$ by volume, the volume of air required is:

$V_{\text{air}} = \dfrac{56}{0.20} = 280\text{ L}$

Answer: $280$

questions.q:
Acrylonitrile ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_3\text{N}$) is a key starting material for the production of acrylic fibres. It can be synthesized from propylene ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_6$) by heating it with nitric oxide ($\text{NO}$) according to the following unbalanced chemical equation:
$\text{C}_3\text{H}_6(g) + \text{NO}(g) \rightarrow \text{C}_3\text{H}_3\text{N}(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(g) + \text{N}_2(g)$

If $105\text{ kg}$ of propylene is reacted with an excess of nitric oxide and the process has an overall yield of $80\%$, what mass of acrylonitrile is obtained?
(Given molar masses in $\text{g mol}^{-1}$: $\text{H} = 1$, $\text{C} = 12$, $\text{N} = 14$, $\text{O} = 16$)
questions.question:
Acrylonitrile ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_3\text{N}$) is a key starting material for the production of acrylic fibres. It can be synthesized from propylene ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_6$) by heating it with nitric oxide ($\text{NO}$) according to the following unbalanced chemical equation:
$\text{C}_3\text{H}_6(g) + \text{NO}(g) \rightarrow \text{C}_3\text{H}_3\text{N}(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(g) + \text{N}_2(g)$

If $105\text{ kg}$ of propylene is reacted with an excess of nitric oxide and the process has an overall yield of $80\%$, what mass of acrylonitrile is obtained?
(Given molar masses in $\text{g mol}^{-1}$: $\text{H} = 1$, $\text{C} = 12$, $\text{N} = 14$, $\text{O} = 16$)
questions.solution:
Balancing the given chemical equation:

$4\text{C}_3\text{H}_6(g) + 6\text{NO}(g) \rightarrow 4\text{C}_3\text{H}_3\text{N}(g) + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}(g) + \text{N}_2(g)$

From the stoichiometry (or by applying the Principle of Atomic Conservation on carbon), $1\text{ mole}$ of propylene ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_6$) produces $1\text{ mole}$ of acrylonitrile ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_3\text{N}$).

Molar mass of $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6 = 3 \times 12 + 6 \times 1 = 42\text{ g mol}^{-1}$
Molar mass of $\text{C}_3\text{H}_3\text{N} = 3 \times 12 + 3 \times 1 + 14 = 53\text{ g mol}^{-1}$

Moles of propylene reacted = $\dfrac{105 \times 10^3\text{ g}}{42\text{ g mol}^{-1}} = 2500\text{ mol}$

Theoretical moles of acrylonitrile produced = $2500\text{ mol}$

Theoretical mass of acrylonitrile = $2500\text{ mol} \times 53\text{ g mol}^{-1} = 132500\text{ g} = 132.5\text{ kg}$

Since the overall yield is $80\%$, the actual mass obtained is:

Actual mass = $132.5\text{ kg} \times \dfrac{80}{100} = 106\text{ kg}$

Answer: $106\text{ kg}$

(Given: Molar masses in $\text{g mol}^{-1}$: $\text{Ag} = 108, \text{C} = 12, \text{O} = 16$)
questions.question:
A sample of $8.28\text{ g}$ of silver carbonate ($\text{Ag}_2\text{CO}_3$) is strongly heated in an open vessel until a constant mass is obtained. The mass of the solid residue left is:
(Given: Molar masses in $\text{g mol}^{-1}$: $\text{Ag} = 108, \text{C} = 12, \text{O} = 16$)
questions.solution:
Molar mass of $\text{Ag}_2\text{CO}_3 = 2 \times 108 + 12 + 3 \times 16 = 276\text{ g mol}^{-1}$

Moles of $\text{Ag}_2\text{CO}_3 = \dfrac{8.28}{276} = 0.03\text{ mol}$

When silver carbonate is strongly heated, it first decomposes into silver oxide and carbon dioxide. However, silver oxide is thermally unstable and further decomposes into silver metal and oxygen gas. The overall reaction is:

$\text{Ag}_2\text{CO}_3(s) \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2\text{Ag}(s) + \text{CO}_2(g) + \dfrac{1}{2}\text{O}_2(g)$

The solid residue left is silver ($\text{Ag}$).

From the stoichiometry of the reaction, $1\text{ mol}$ of $\text{Ag}_2\text{CO}_3$ yields $2\text{ mol}$ of $\text{Ag}$.

Moles of $\text{Ag}$ formed = $2 \times 0.03 = 0.06\text{ mol}$

Mass of solid residue ($\text{Ag}$) = $0.06 \times 108 = 6.48\text{ g}$

Answer: $6.48\text{ g}$

questions.q:
Detonating gas is a mixture of hydrogen and oxygen gases in a $2:1$ molar ratio. The volume of detonating gas produced at $0^{\circ}\text{C}$ and $1\text{ atm}$ from the complete electrolytic decomposition of $0.20\text{ mol}$ of liquid water is:
(Given: Molar volume of an ideal gas at $0^{\circ}\text{C}$ and $1\text{ atm}$ is $22.4\text{ L mol}^{-1}$)
questions.question:
Detonating gas is a mixture of hydrogen and oxygen gases in a $2:1$ molar ratio. The volume of detonating gas produced at $0^{\circ}\text{C}$ and $1\text{ atm}$ from the complete electrolytic decomposition of $0.20\text{ mol}$ of liquid water is:
(Given: Molar volume of an ideal gas at $0^{\circ}\text{C}$ and $1\text{ atm}$ is $22.4\text{ L mol}^{-1}$)
questions.solution:
The electrolytic decomposition of water is given by the equation:

$2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2(g) + \text{O}_2(g)$

From the stoichiometry of the reaction, $2\text{ mol}$ of water produces $2\text{ mol}$ of $\text{H}_2$ and $1\text{ mol}$ of $\text{O}_2$.

For $0.20\text{ mol}$ of water, the moles of gases produced are:

Moles of $\text{H}_2 = 0.20\text{ mol}$

Moles of $\text{O}_2 = 0.10\text{ mol}$

Total moles of detonating gas $= 0.20 + 0.10 = 0.30\text{ mol}$

The molar volume of an ideal gas at $0^{\circ}\text{C}$ and $1\text{ atm}$ is $22.4\text{ L mol}^{-1}$.

Volume of detonating gas $= 0.30 \times 22.4 = 6.72\text{ L}$

Answer: $6.72\text{ L}$

questions.q:
What mass of solid ammonium carbamate ($\text{NH}_2\text{COONH}_4$), when vaporised at $273^{\circ}\text{C}$ and $1\text{ atm}$ pressure, will produce a total gas volume of $13.44\text{ L}$? Assume that the solid completely decomposes as:
$\text{NH}_2\text{COONH}_4(\text{s}) \rightarrow \text{CO}_2(\text{g}) + 2\text{NH}_3(\text{g})$
[Assume ideal gas behaviour and that the molar volume of an ideal gas at $273\text{ K}$ and $1\text{ atm}$ is $22.4\text{ L}$]
questions.question:
What mass of solid ammonium carbamate ($\text{NH}_2\text{COONH}_4$), when vaporised at $273^{\circ}\text{C}$ and $1\text{ atm}$ pressure, will produce a total gas volume of $13.44\text{ L}$? Assume that the solid completely decomposes as:
$\text{NH}_2\text{COONH}_4(\text{s}) \rightarrow \text{CO}_2(\text{g}) + 2\text{NH}_3(\text{g})$
[Assume ideal gas behaviour and that the molar volume of an ideal gas at $273\text{ K}$ and $1\text{ atm}$ is $22.4\text{ L}$]
questions.solution:
The given decomposition reaction is:
$\text{NH}_2\text{COONH}_4(\text{s}) \rightarrow \text{CO}_2(\text{g}) + 2\text{NH}_3(\text{g})$

From the stoichiometry of the reaction, $1\text{ mole}$ of solid ammonium carbamate produces $1 + 2 = 3\text{ moles}$ of gaseous products.

The total volume of the gas mixture is $13.44\text{ L}$ at $273^{\circ}\text{C}$ ($546\text{ K}$) and $1\text{ atm}$.

The molar volume of an ideal gas at $273\text{ K}$ and $1\text{ atm}$ is $22.4\text{ L}$.
At $546\text{ K}$ and $1\text{ atm}$, the molar volume is $22.4 \times \dfrac{546}{273} = 44.8\text{ L}$.

The total number of moles of gas produced is:
$n_{gas} = \dfrac{13.44}{44.8} = 0.3\text{ mol}$

Since $3\text{ moles}$ of gas are produced from $1\text{ mole}$ of solid, the number of moles of ammonium carbamate decomposed is:
$n_{solid} = \dfrac{0.3}{3} = 0.1\text{ mol}$

The molar mass of ammonium carbamate ($\text{NH}_2\text{COONH}_4$) is:
$M = 14 + 2 + 12 + 16 + 16 + 14 + 4 = 78\text{ g/mol}$

The mass of ammonium carbamate required is:
$m = 0.1 \times 78 = 7.8\text{ g}$

Answer: $7.8\text{ g}$

(B) The number of moles of $\text{H}_2$ gas evolved with excess aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ is $0.2\text{ mol}$.

questions.question:

(A) The number of moles of $\text{H}_2$ gas evolved with excess dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is $0.3\text{ mol}$.
(B) The number of moles of $\text{H}_2$ gas evolved with excess aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ is $0.2\text{ mol}$.

(D) The mass of $\text{H}_2$ gas produced in each case is $0.6\text{ g}$.

questions.solution:
